summary: Module 4 FIX: precise fix prompt for the IDOR + review of the landed fix. Step 1 -- vulnerability identified precisely: POST /teams/{team_id}/invitations must verify owner-or-admin membership between authentication and invitation creation; the URL team_id must never be treated as authorization. Step 2 -- the fix prompt (good-prompt style, shown side-by-side against the bad 'fix the security issue' prompt): it named the exact file (app/routers/team_router.py), the exact endpoint (POST /teams/{team_id}/invitations), the exact check (reuse teams_service.require_owner_or_admin which queries teams.created_by == caller OR team_members.role == 'admin'), the error contract (403 via HTTPException -> error_envelope), and explicitly said what NOT to change (accept endpoint keeps token-based authorization; no refactor of existing member endpoints). Step 3 -- review of the landed fix confirms substance, not placeholder: require_owner_or_admin (teams_service.py:56) is a real query -- it fetches the team via db.get and queries team_members via select(TeamMember).where(team_id, user_id), returning 403 unless owner or role == 'admin'; NOT a 'const isAdmin = true' placeholder. The guard is placed at team_router.py:133 (before any DB insert), :162 (list), and require_owner at :186 (revoke). Nothing else in the endpoints changed. VERIFICATION: m4_idor_probe.py 9 cases -- Bob (non-member) create/list/revoke all 403; owner create 201; dup pending 409; owner revoke 204; accept revoked 400; accept once 200; accept replay 400. The lesson is the module's own: a specific prompt with schema context produces a substantive guard; a vague prompt produces a placeholder or a refactor. My M2 interface-contract discipline (embedding actual schema + ownership rules) is exactly what prevented the placeholder failure.
evidence: teams_service.py:56 require_owner_or_admin real DB query (db.get team + select TeamMember)
m4_idor_probe.py: 9/9 cases, IDOR closed, replay blocked, nothing else changed
